newsitem.title: USA: AT&T simplifies card plan, adds payphone fee.
newsitem.headline: AT&T simplifies card plan, adds payphone fee.

text.p: AT&T Corp. on Friday introduced a flat, 35-cent per-minute charge for phone calls using its AT&T calling card and cut the surcharges customers pay for connecting to the AT&T network, a spokeswoman said.

Separately, the leading U.S. long-distance carrier said it will add a 35-cent charge for coinless calls made from pay phones over the AT&T network in order to meet new U.S. regulations. The added charge takes effect June 1.

The charge is designed to offset compensation payments it and other long-distance carriers are now required to make to pay phone operators according to a Federal Communications Commission order handed down last fall.
AT&T said the company will see no benefit from its new 35-cent pay phone fee and additional charges it leveled on business customers earlier this year.
All revenue collected by AT&T from these fees will be used to offset rebates it is paying to pay phone operators. "Not a nickel will land in our pockets," an AT&T spokeswoman said.
AT&T has had business customers, not consumers, bear the lion's share of the burden for the pay phone compensation, according to industry sources.
In February, AT&T boosted "800" number rates by 3 percent for incoming customer calls and added a 15-cent-per-call surcharge on business calling cards.
On May 1, it raised rates for interstate toll-free service 7 percent and for outgoing business calls by 2 percent.

AT&T spokeswoman Karyn Vaughn-Fritz said the switch to per-minute charges has replaced a complicated hodgepodge of up to 66 factors previously used to set pricing, including the time of day of the call and the distance it travelled.
The switch to per-minute pricing, combined with the lower network surcharge costs, will mean a 1 percent overall cut in an average AT&T consumer's costs, Vaughn-Fritz said.

In a move analysts said was designed to shore up AT&T customer loyalty, calling card customers dialing a special "800" number (1-800-CALL-ATT) will pay a one-time network access charge of 35 cents, down from the prior 90-cent surcharge. AT&T card customers direct dialing using the 0+ prefix will pay a 60-cent surcharge, down from 90 cents.
AT&T's consumer calling card pricing comes at a premium to many of its competitors in the industry. For example, Sprint Corp.'s FonCard runs 25 cents a minute and has no surcharges.
AT&T commands the higher pricing by offering a set of premium services not available from rivals such as beefed-up fraud detection and simplified dialing plans, analysts said.
AT&T consumer card price changes became effective Tuesday.

The FCC order calls on 20 long-distance operators to refund about $1 billion to pay phone operators. AT&T must shoulder a little over 50 percent of that amount, reflecting AT&T's estimated share of the pay phone long distance market.
AT&T gained 37.5 cents to close at $36.75 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
